title: Seoul Lunch Habits: What Koreans Actually Eat for Lunch Today

content:
📅 Updated 2026.08.28
Key takeaways
  • Most Korean salarymen eat quick, affordable, and often shared meals at local restaurants near their office.
  • Convenience store *dosirak* (lunchboxes) or *gimbap* are popular for busy days or budget-conscious eaters.
  • While trends come and go, hearty stews and rice dishes remain the staple for a typical weekday lunch as of August 27, 2026.
👤 This is for readers who are planning to visit, move to, or simply want an authentic glimpse into the daily lunch routines of people in Seoul, Korea.

You’re scrolling through Instagram, seeing all the vibrant Korean food, the cute cafes, the sizzling BBQ. Naturally, you wonder: what do Koreans actually eat for lunch when they’re not posing for photos? As of August 27, 2026, the short answer is usually something quick, affordable, and hearty from a small restaurant near the office, or sometimes a grab-and-go convenience store meal. It's not always glamorous, but it’s real.

The Ubiquitous Office Area Restaurant Lunch

Walk into any office district in Seoul around 12 PM, and you'll see a flood of salarymen and women pouring out of buildings, heading straight for the countless small eateries. This is where the magic (or rather, the routine) happens. We're talking baekban (a set meal with rice, soup, and various side dishes), kimchi jjigae (kimchi stew), doenjang jjigae (soybean paste stew), and sundubu jjigae (soft tofu stew). These are our go-to comfort foods. They’re served fast, they’re hot, and they hit the spot. Prices usually range from 8,000 to 12,000 won (roughly $6-$9 USD). The goal is efficiency: get in, eat, get out, often within 30-40 minutes. In my office, we usually decide as a team where to go, sometimes rotating our favorite spots. We’ll often order different stews and share the side dishes (banchan), which often include kimchi, bean sprouts, and various pickled vegetables. It’s a collective dining experience, even if we’re just discussing work.

Point: It's less about gourmet and more about satisfying, shared efficiency.

The Lifesaver: Convenience Store Lunches & Quick Bites

Let’s be honest, not every day allows for a sit-down meal. Sometimes, a deadline looms, or you just can’t face another jjigae. That’s when the convenience store, or pyeonijeom (literally 'convenience store'), becomes our best friend. Their dosirak (lunchboxes) have really upped their game in recent years, offering everything from simple fried rice with a side of sausage to more elaborate meals with grilled fish or bulgogi. Prices are fantastic, usually between 4,500 and 7,000 won ($3.50-$5.50 USD). Add a samgak gimbap (triangle seaweed rice roll) for 1,200-2,000 won, maybe a cup of instant ramyeon (ramen noodles), and you’ve got a quick, cheap, and surprisingly filling lunch. I've definitely had my share of convenience store dosirak eaten at my desk, hunched over a keyboard. It’s not ideal, but it’s a perfectly acceptable solution when time is precious. The variety means you can almost always find something new, too.

Point: Quick, cheap, and surprisingly varied, convenience store lunches are a practical necessity for the busy salaryman.

Trend Chasers: Cafes and International Flavors

While the traditional fare reigns supreme, Seoul is a city of trends. Younger office workers, especially, are always on the hunt for something new or a different vibe. You’ll see plenty of people opting for lunch at cafes, grabbing a sandwich, a salad, or a light pasta dish. Bakeries are also popular, offering savory pastries or simple bread. International food, from Japanese ramen to Italian pasta or even American-style burgers, has carved out its own niche in lunch culture. These options tend to be a bit pricier, often 12,000-20,000 won ($9-$15 USD), and usually take longer. It’s less about fueling up quickly and more about enjoying the meal or the atmosphere. My younger team members are constantly sending links to newly opened 'brunch' spots, though true brunch is more of a weekend thing for us. Honestly, some of these trendy places are overhyped, but they do offer a nice change of pace now and then.

Point: While not the daily norm, modern cafes and international dishes offer a refreshing, albeit pricier, alternative to traditional Korean lunch.

Lunch Price Tag: What to Expect in Seoul in 2026

Understanding the cost of lunch is key for visitors or those considering moving here. As of mid-2026, you can generally categorize lunch prices as follows:

Small Local Eateries (e.g., jjigae, baekban*): Expect to pay between 8,000 KRW and 12,000 KRW per person. This is the most common and budget-friendly option for a sit-down meal.

Convenience Stores (dosirak, gimbap): These are the cheapest, ranging from 4,500 KRW to 7,000 KRW for a full meal, or 1,200 KRW to 3,000 KRW for a samgak gimbap or a cup of ramyeon*. You can get a decent lunch for under 7,000 KRW easily.

* Cafes and Trendier Spots (e.g., sandwiches, pasta, salads): These will set you back more, typically 12,000 KRW to 20,000 KRW, sometimes more if you add a fancy drink. It’s a splurge for lunch.

* Company Cafeterias/Food Courts: Many larger companies or office buildings have their own cafeterias, often subsidized. My office building has a food court with several options, usually priced around 7,000 KRW to 10,000 KRW, offering a variety of Korean and sometimes international dishes. These are great for consistency and speed.

Overall, a solid, satisfying Korean lunch will generally cost you somewhere between 8,000 and 12,000 won. This hasn't changed drastically in the last few years, though everything feels like it's creeping up a bit.

Point: Budget around 10,000 won for a typical, good Korean lunch; convenience stores offer cheaper alternatives, and trendy spots are pricier.

Lunchtime Culture and Etiquette: More Than Just Eating

Lunch in Korea isn't just about the food; it's also about the social dynamics and unspoken rules. The palli-palli (hurry-hurry, do-it-now mindset) is very evident. Restaurants are designed for quick turnover. You'll often share dishes, especially the banchan, and it's common for one person (often the most senior, or whoever suggests the place) to pay for the entire group, especially if it's a team lunch. There’s a subtle dance of who reaches for the card first. Don't be surprised if your colleagues insist on paying – it's a gesture of camaraderie. After the meal, it's also common to grab coffee, either at a nearby cafe or from a vending machine, before heading back to work. This mini-break is part of the routine. At my first company lunch, I accidentally started serving myself the banchan before others had picked up their chopsticks – a small nunchi (the art of reading the room) misstep. Best to wait and see what others do.

Point: Lunch is a fast-paced, communal affair with unspoken rules of sharing and generosity, deeply rooted in Korea's palli-palli culture.

The Hoesik Lunch: A Rare but Memorable Occurrence

While hoesik (the after-work company dinner) is the norm, a 'lunch hoesik' does happen on occasion. These are usually for special team celebrations, a project completion, or when someone is leaving. Instead of the usual quick stew, a lunch hoesik might involve something more elaborate, like galbi (grilled ribs) or a larger budaegge jjigae (army base stew) where everyone cooks together. These are less about efficiency and more about bonding and enjoying a richer meal. They're definitely not a daily occurrence, maybe a few times a year for my team. The atmosphere is more relaxed, and the conversations tend to be less work-focused. It's a nice break from the usual routine, but it's important to understand it's an exception, not the rule, for what Koreans actually eat for lunch.

Point: A 'lunch hoesik' is a rare, special occasion for team bonding, not typical daily fare for most salarymen.

Stuff you're probably wondering

Q. Do Koreans eat Korean BBQ for lunch?

A. While delicious, Korean BBQ (*gogi-gui*) is typically a dinner meal due to the time it takes to cook and eat. A 'lunch hoesik' (company dinner) might occasionally feature it, but it's not a common daily lunch for most salarymen.

Q. How much does a typical lunch cost in Seoul in 2026?

A. As of 2026, a standard sit-down lunch at a local eatery in Seoul typically costs between 8,000 and 12,000 won (roughly $6-$9 USD). Convenience store options are cheaper, usually 4,500-7,000 won.

Q. What is *dosirak*?

A. *Dosirak* is a Korean lunchbox, similar to a bento box. Modern convenience store *dosirak* offer pre-packaged meals with rice, a main dish like bulgogi or fried chicken, and various side dishes, perfect for a quick, affordable lunch.

Q. Is it common for Koreans to eat lunch alone?

A. While group lunches with colleagues are very common, eating alone (*honbap*) has become increasingly acceptable, especially with the rise of convenience store meals and single-person restaurants. It's not unusual, but group dining is still the norm in office settings.

Q. Do Koreans often eat Western food for lunch?

A. Yes, especially among younger generations and in trendy areas, Western options like sandwiches, pasta, and salads are popular lunch choices. However, traditional Korean dishes remain the staple for daily office lunches due to their affordability, speed, and comfort.

서울 점심 식사 습관: 오늘날 한국인들이 실제로 점심으로 무엇을 먹는가

인스타그램을 스크롤하며 활기찬 한국 음식, 귀여운 카페, 지글거리는 바비큐를 보고 있습니다. 당연히 궁금할 것입니다. 한국인들은 사진을 찍기 위해 포즈를 취하지 않을 때 *실제로* 점심으로 무엇을 먹을까요? 2026년 8월 27일 현재, 간단히 말해 보통 사무실 근처 작은 식당에서 빠르고 저렴하며 든든한 음식을 먹거나, 때로는 편의점에서 간편하게 사 먹는 식사입니다. 항상 화려하지는 않지만, 이것이 현실입니다.

## 흔하디흔한 오피스 지역 식당 점심

정오쯤 서울의 어느 오피스 지구에 가보면, 수많은 직장인들이 건물에서 쏟아져 나와 셀 수 없이 많은 작은 식당으로 향하는 모습을 볼 수 있을 것입니다. 이곳에서 마법(혹은 일상)이 일어납니다. *백반*(밥, 국, 다양한 반찬으로 구성된 정식), *김치찌개*, *된장찌개*, *순두부찌개* 같은 것들을 말합니다. 이것들이 우리가 즐겨 찾는 편안한 음식입니다. 빨리 나오고, 뜨겁고, 딱 좋습니다. 가격은 보통 8,000원에서 12,000원(대략 6~9달러) 사이입니다. 목표는 효율성입니다. 들어가서 먹고, 나가는 것이며, 종종 30~40분 안에 끝납니다. 제 사무실에서는 보통 팀원들과 함께 어디로 갈지 결정하고, 때로는 우리가 좋아하는 장소를 번갈아 갑니다. 우리는 종종 다른 찌개를 주문하고 *반찬*(김치, 콩나물, 다양한 절임 채소 등이 포함됨)을 공유합니다. 비록 업무에 대해 이야기할 뿐이지만, 이것은 공동 식사 경험입니다.

> 요점: 미식보다는 만족스럽고 효율적인 공유 식사에 가깝습니다.

## 구세주: 편의점 점심 및 간편식

솔직히 말해서, 매일 앉아서 식사할 수 있는 것은 아닙니다. 때로는 마감 기한이 다가오거나, 또 다른 *찌개*를 먹고 싶지 않을 때가 있습니다. 그때 편의점, 즉 *편의점*이 우리의 가장 친한 친구가 됩니다. 편의점의 *도시락*은 최근 몇 년간 정말 발전하여, 간단한 소시지 볶음밥부터 구운 생선이나 불고기가 포함된 더 정교한 식사까지 모든 것을 제공합니다. 가격은 환상적이며, 보통 4,500원에서 7,000원(3.50~5.50달러) 사이입니다. 1,200~2,000원짜리 *삼각김밥* 하나, 어쩌면 인스턴트 *라면* 한 컵을 추가하면 빠르고 저렴하며 놀랍도록 든든한 점심이 됩니다. 저는 키보드에 웅크린 채 책상에서 편의점 *도시락*을 먹었던 경험이 많습니다. 이상적이지는 않지만, 시간이 귀할 때 완벽하게 받아들일 수 있는 해결책입니다. 다양한 종류 덕분에 거의 항상 새로운 것을 찾을 수 있습니다.

> 요점: 빠르고 저렴하며 놀랍도록 다양한 편의점 점심은 바쁜 직장인에게 실용적인 필수품입니다.

## 트렌드 추종자: 카페 및 국제적인 맛

전통적인 음식이 최고를 차지하고 있지만, 서울은 트렌드의 도시입니다. 특히 젊은 직장인들은 항상 새로운 것이나 다른 분위기를 찾아다닙니다. 많은 사람들이 카페에서 점심을 먹으며 샌드위치, 샐러드 또는 가벼운 파스타 요리를 선택하는 것을 볼 수 있을 것입니다. 베이커리도 인기가 많으며, 짭짤한 페이스트리나 간단한 빵을 제공합니다. 일본 라멘부터 이탈리아 파스타, 심지어 미국식 버거에 이르기까지 국제 음식은 점심 문화에서 자체적인 틈새시장을 개척했습니다. 이러한 옵션은 가격이 조금 더 비싸서 종종 12,000원에서 20,000원(9~15달러)이며, 보통 더 오래 걸립니다. 빨리 배를 채우는 것보다는 식사나 분위기를 즐기는 데 더 중점을 둡니다. 제 젊은 팀원들은 새로 오픈한 '브런치' 장소 링크를 끊임없이 보내지만, 진정한 브런치는 우리에게 주말에 더 가깝습니다. 솔직히, 이러한 트렌디한 장소 중 일부는 과대평가되었지만, 가끔 기분 전환을 제공합니다.

> 요점: 매일의 일상은 아니지만, 현대적인 카페와 국제 요리는 전통적인 한국 점심에 대한 신선하고 비싸지만 대안을 제공합니다.

## 점심 가격표: 2026년 서울에서 예상할 수 있는 것

점심 비용을 이해하는 것은 방문객이나 이곳으로 이사를 고려하는 사람들에게 중요합니다. 2026년 중반 현재, 점심 가격은 일반적으로 다음과 같이 분류할 수 있습니다.

*   **작은 동네 식당(예: *찌개*, *백반*):** 1인당 8,000원에서 12,000원 사이를 예상하세요. 이것은 앉아서 먹는 식사 중 가장 흔하고 예산 친화적인 옵션입니다.
*   **편의점(*도시락*, *김밥*):** 가장 저렴하며, 한 끼 식사에 4,500원에서 7,000원, 또는 *삼각김밥*이나 *라면* 한 컵에 1,200원에서 3,000원입니다. 7,000원 미만으로 괜찮은 점심을 쉽게 먹을 수 있습니다.
*   **카페 및 트렌디한 장소(예: 샌드위치, 파스타, 샐러드):** 더 많은 비용이 들며, 일반적으로 12,000원에서 20,000원, 고급 음료를 추가하면 더 비쌀 수도 있습니다. 점심으로는 사치입니다.
*   **회사 구내식당/푸드코트:** 많은 대기업이나 오피스 빌딩에는 자체 구내식당이 있으며, 종종 보조금을 받습니다. 제 사무실 건물에는 여러 옵션이 있는 푸드코트가 있으며, 보통 7,000원에서 10,000원 사이로 다양한 한식과 때로는 국제 요리를 제공합니다. 이것들은 일관성과 속도 면에서 훌륭합니다.

전반적으로, 든든하고 만족스러운 한국 점심은 일반적으로 8,000원에서 12,000원 사이의 비용이 듭니다. 지난 몇 년 동안 크게 변하지는 않았지만, 모든 것이 조금씩 오르는 것 같습니다.

> 요점: 일반적인 좋은 한국 점심은 약 10,000원 정도를 예산으로 잡으세요. 편의점은 더 저렴한 대안을 제공하고, 트렌디한 장소는 더 비쌉니다.

## 점심시간 문화와 에티켓: 단순히 먹는 것 이상

한국에서 점심은 단순히 음식에 관한 것이 아닙니다. 사회적 역동성과 암묵적인 규칙에 관한 것이기도 합니다. *빨리빨리*(서둘러, 지금 당장 하라는 사고방식) 문화가 매우 분명합니다. 식당은 빠른 회전을 위해 설계되었습니다. 종종 요리, 특히 *반찬*을 공유하며, 한 사람(종종 가장 선임자 또는 장소를 제안한 사람)이 전체 그룹의 식사비를 지불하는 것이 일반적입니다. 특히 팀 점심인 경우 더욱 그렇습니다. 누가 먼저 카드를 꺼낼지에 대한 미묘한 줄다리기가 있습니다. 동료들이 계산하겠다고 고집해도 놀라지 마세요. 그것은 동료애의 표현입니다. 식사 후에는 근처 카페나 자판기에서 커피를 마시고 다시 일하러 가는 것이 일반적입니다. 이 짧은 휴식은 일상의 일부입니다. 첫 회사 점심 때, 저는 다른 사람들이 젓가락을 들기 전에 실수로 *반찬*을 스스로 덜어 먹기 시작했습니다. 작은 *눈치*(상황을 읽는 기술) 실책이었습니다. 다른 사람들이 무엇을 하는지 기다려보는 것이 가장 좋습니다.

> 요점: 점심은 한국의 *빨리빨리* 문화에 깊이 뿌리내린, 공유와 관대함의 암묵적인 규칙이 있는 빠르게 진행되는 공동체적인 행사입니다.

## 회식 점심: 드물지만 기억에 남는 행사

*회식*(퇴근 후 회사 저녁 식사)이 일반적이지만, '점심 회식'도 가끔 발생합니다. 이것은 보통 특별한 팀 축하, 프로젝트 완료 또는 누군가가 떠날 때입니다. 일반적인 빠른 찌개 대신, 점심 *회식*은 *갈비*(구운 갈비)나 모두가 함께 요리하는 더 큰 *부대찌개*와 같이 더 정교한 것을 포함할 수 있습니다. 이것들은 효율성보다는 유대감을 형성하고 더 풍성한 식사를 즐기는 데 중점을 둡니다. 제 팀의 경우 매일 일어나는 일은 아니며, 1년에 몇 번 정도입니다. 분위기는 더 편안하고, 대화는 업무 중심적이지 않은 경향이 있습니다. 평소 일상에서 벗어나는 좋은 휴식이지만, 이것이 한국인들이 실제로 점심으로 무엇을 먹는지에 대한 예외이지 규칙은 아니라는 것을 이해하는 것이 중요합니다.

> 요점: '점심 회식'은 팀 유대감을 위한 드물고 특별한 행사이며, 대부분의 직장인에게는 전형적인 일상 식사가 아닙니다.
content_raw:
You’re scrolling through Instagram, seeing all the vibrant Korean food, the cute cafes, the sizzling BBQ. Naturally, you wonder: what do Koreans actually eat for lunch when they’re not posing for photos? As of August 27, 2026, the short answer is usually something quick, affordable, and hearty from a small restaurant near the office, or sometimes a grab-and-go convenience store meal. It's not always glamorous, but it’s real.

## The Ubiquitous Office Area Restaurant Lunch

Walk into any office district in Seoul around 12 PM, and you'll see a flood of salarymen and women pouring out of buildings, heading straight for the countless small eateries. This is where the magic (or rather, the routine) happens. We're talking baekban (a set meal with rice, soup, and various side dishes), kimchi jjigae (kimchi stew), doenjang jjigae (soybean paste stew), and sundubu jjigae (soft tofu stew). These are our go-to comfort foods. They’re served fast, they’re hot, and they hit the spot. Prices usually range from 8,000 to 12,000 won (roughly $6-$9 USD). The goal is efficiency: get in, eat, get out, often within 30-40 minutes. In my office, we usually decide as a team where to go, sometimes rotating our favorite spots. We’ll often order different stews and share the side dishes (banchan), which often include kimchi, bean sprouts, and various pickled vegetables. It’s a collective dining experience, even if we’re just discussing work.

> Point: It's less about gourmet and more about satisfying, shared efficiency.

## The Lifesaver: Convenience Store Lunches & Quick Bites

Let’s be honest, not every day allows for a sit-down meal. Sometimes, a deadline looms, or you just can’t face another jjigae. That’s when the convenience store, or pyeonijeom (literally 'convenience store'), becomes our best friend. Their dosirak (lunchboxes) have really upped their game in recent years, offering everything from simple fried rice with a side of sausage to more elaborate meals with grilled fish or bulgogi. Prices are fantastic, usually between 4,500 and 7,000 won ($3.50-$5.50 USD). Add a samgak gimbap (triangle seaweed rice roll) for 1,200-2,000 won, maybe a cup of instant ramyeon (ramen noodles), and you’ve got a quick, cheap, and surprisingly filling lunch. I've definitely had my share of convenience store dosirak eaten at my desk, hunched over a keyboard. It’s not ideal, but it’s a perfectly acceptable solution when time is precious. The variety means you can almost always find something new, too.

> Point: Quick, cheap, and surprisingly varied, convenience store lunches are a practical necessity for the busy salaryman.

## Trend Chasers: Cafes and International Flavors

While the traditional fare reigns supreme, Seoul is a city of trends. Younger office workers, especially, are always on the hunt for something new or a different vibe. You’ll see plenty of people opting for lunch at cafes, grabbing a sandwich, a salad, or a light pasta dish. Bakeries are also popular, offering savory pastries or simple bread. International food, from Japanese ramen to Italian pasta or even American-style burgers, has carved out its own niche in lunch culture. These options tend to be a bit pricier, often 12,000-20,000 won ($9-$15 USD), and usually take longer. It’s less about fueling up quickly and more about enjoying the meal or the atmosphere. My younger team members are constantly sending links to newly opened 'brunch' spots, though true brunch is more of a weekend thing for us. Honestly, some of these trendy places are overhyped, but they do offer a nice change of pace now and then.

> Point: While not the daily norm, modern cafes and international dishes offer a refreshing, albeit pricier, alternative to traditional Korean lunch.

## Lunch Price Tag: What to Expect in Seoul in 2026

Understanding the cost of lunch is key for visitors or those considering moving here. As of mid-2026, you can generally categorize lunch prices as follows:

   Small Local Eateries (e.g., jjigae, baekban*): Expect to pay between 8,000 KRW and 12,000 KRW per person. This is the most common and budget-friendly option for a sit-down meal.
   Convenience Stores (dosirak, gimbap): These are the cheapest, ranging from 4,500 KRW to 7,000 KRW for a full meal, or 1,200 KRW to 3,000 KRW for a samgak gimbap or a cup of ramyeon*. You can get a decent lunch for under 7,000 KRW easily.
*   Cafes and Trendier Spots (e.g., sandwiches, pasta, salads): These will set you back more, typically 12,000 KRW to 20,000 KRW, sometimes more if you add a fancy drink. It’s a splurge for lunch.
*   Company Cafeterias/Food Courts: Many larger companies or office buildings have their own cafeterias, often subsidized. My office building has a food court with several options, usually priced around 7,000 KRW to 10,000 KRW, offering a variety of Korean and sometimes international dishes. These are great for consistency and speed.

Overall, a solid, satisfying Korean lunch will generally cost you somewhere between 8,000 and 12,000 won. This hasn't changed drastically in the last few years, though everything feels like it's creeping up a bit.

> Point: Budget around 10,000 won for a typical, good Korean lunch; convenience stores offer cheaper alternatives, and trendy spots are pricier.

## Lunchtime Culture and Etiquette: More Than Just Eating

Lunch in Korea isn't just about the food; it's also about the social dynamics and unspoken rules. The palli-palli (hurry-hurry, do-it-now mindset) is very evident. Restaurants are designed for quick turnover. You'll often share dishes, especially the banchan, and it's common for one person (often the most senior, or whoever suggests the place) to pay for the entire group, especially if it's a team lunch. There’s a subtle dance of who reaches for the card first. Don't be surprised if your colleagues insist on paying – it's a gesture of camaraderie. After the meal, it's also common to grab coffee, either at a nearby cafe or from a vending machine, before heading back to work. This mini-break is part of the routine. At my first company lunch, I accidentally started serving myself the banchan before others had picked up their chopsticks – a small nunchi (the art of reading the room) misstep. Best to wait and see what others do.

> Point: Lunch is a fast-paced, communal affair with unspoken rules of sharing and generosity, deeply rooted in Korea's palli-palli culture.

## The Hoesik Lunch: A Rare but Memorable Occurrence

While hoesik (the after-work company dinner) is the norm, a 'lunch hoesik' does happen on occasion. These are usually for special team celebrations, a project completion, or when someone is leaving. Instead of the usual quick stew, a lunch hoesik might involve something more elaborate, like galbi (grilled ribs) or a larger budaegge jjigae (army base stew) where everyone cooks together. These are less about efficiency and more about bonding and enjoying a richer meal. They're definitely not a daily occurrence, maybe a few times a year for my team. The atmosphere is more relaxed, and the conversations tend to be less work-focused. It's a nice break from the usual routine, but it's important to understand it's an exception, not the rule, for what Koreans actually eat for lunch.

> Point: A 'lunch hoesik' is a rare, special occasion for team bonding, not typical daily fare for most salarymen.

mainEntity.name: Do Koreans eat Korean BBQ for lunch?

acceptedAnswer.text: While delicious, Korean BBQ (*gogi-gui*) is typically a dinner meal due to the time it takes to cook and eat. A 'lunch hoesik' (company dinner) might occasionally feature it, but it's not a common daily lunch for most salarymen.

mainEntity.name: How much does a typical lunch cost in Seoul in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: As of 2026, a standard sit-down lunch at a local eatery in Seoul typically costs between 8,000 and 12,000 won (roughly $6-$9 USD). Convenience store options are cheaper, usually 4,500-7,000 won.

*Dosirak* is a Korean lunchbox, similar to a bento box. Modern convenience store *dosirak* offer pre-packaged meals with rice, a main dish like bulgogi or fried chicken, and various side dishes, perfect for a quick, affordable lunch.

mainEntity.name: Is it common for Koreans to eat lunch alone?

acceptedAnswer.text: While group lunches with colleagues are very common, eating alone (*honbap*) has become increasingly acceptable, especially with the rise of convenience store meals and single-person restaurants. It's not unusual, but group dining is still the norm in office settings.

mainEntity.name: Do Koreans often eat Western food for lunch?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, especially among younger generations and in trendy areas, Western options like sandwiches, pasta, and salads are popular lunch choices. However, traditional Korean dishes remain the staple for daily office lunches due to their affordability, speed, and comfort.
